findings.title: The home page never says what the bakery sells
findings.description: The hero heading and subheading are a brand slogan. No product noun (cake, pastry, bread) and no primary action appear in the first heading, subheading or first 150 words.
findings.user_impact: Visitors cannot tell whether this is a bakery, a restaurant or a cookery school, so some leave before finding the order path and the rest guess where to click.
findings.root_cause: The home page hero names the brand story instead of the product, which leaves first-time visitors unable to say what is offered.
findings.intended_behavior: The hero is meant to create a warm artisan impression; that works only after a visitor already knows the business sells cakes.

evidence.description: In the five-second test the first-time visitor could not say whether the site sells bread, cakes, classes or something else.
The low-literacy persona guessed a restaurant and said she would not know where to click to order.
CL-01 fails: no noun naming the product appears in the heading, subheading or first 150 words.

steps: Read only the first heading, the subheading and the primary navigation labels.
Write down what the business sells.
reproduction.expected: The visitor names the product (custom cakes and pastries) within five seconds.
reproduction.actual: Visitors name a lifestyle, a restaurant, or nothing.

impact.reason: Visitors can still explore, but they cannot tell what is offered or what to do first.

frequency.reason: Every visitor lands on the hero.

persistence.reason: Once a visitor learns what the business sells, the page stops being confusing.

confidence.reason: Three independent sessions reached the same conclusion from the same text.

findings.baseline_comparison: Bakery and food-shop sites conventionally name the product in the first heading; this site uses a brand slogan only.

remediation.strategy: Replace the hero heading with a sentence naming the product and the audience, and add one primary button toward ordering.

copy_changes.after: Custom cakes and pastries for your celebrations

gap.intended: Inferred goal: collect custom cake order inquiries.
gap.perceived: A brand story with no visible product and no visible action.

verification.notes: Re-fetched the home page: hero text unchanged and no product noun in the first 150 words.

findings.title: Menu labels are brand-speak and hide the ordering path
findings.description: The main navigation uses 'Our Craft', 'Collections' and 'Atelier'. Custom cake ordering sits under Atelier > Bespoke Orders, and no header button points to it.
findings.user_impact: Visitors who want to order must guess which label leads there. One persona needed eight steps for a three-step task and another signed up for the newsletter believing it was the order form.
findings.root_cause: The main menu names sections after the brand's own vocabulary, which sends customers to the wrong page when they look for cakes or ordering.
findings.intended_behavior: The labels are meant to feel premium and consistent with the brand; they work only for people who already know the business.

evidence.description: The first-time visitor opened Atelier hoping for ordering and found a photo page with no ordering information.
The low-literacy persona signed up for the newsletter believing it was how to order a cake.
NN-2 fails: none of the five labels uses the words customers use when they look for cakes or ordering.

steps: Without reading anything else, choose the menu item you expect to lead to ordering a birthday cake.
Follow it and note where you end up.
reproduction.expected: The first click lands on a page about ordering a cake, in three steps or fewer.
reproduction.actual: The first click lands on Collections or Atelier; reaching Bespoke Orders took eight steps for one persona and was never reached by another.

impact.reason: One persona completed the wrong action instead of the order.

frequency.reason: Two of the three personas were affected on the site's primary task.

persistence.reason: Once the path is learned it is easy, but most visitors arrive without that knowledge.

confidence.reason: Three independent sessions, including one lens audit, point at the same labels.

findings.baseline_comparison: Local shop sites conventionally label the ordering route in plain words ('Order a cake', 'Cakes') and keep a persistent order button in the header.

remediation.strategy: Rename the menu items in customer vocabulary and add a persistent 'Order a cake' button in the header.

verification.notes: One of three personas completed the task, so the problem slows and misleads users rather than preventing the task outright.

findings.title: No phone number, email or address to contact the business
findings.description: The contact page offers a form only. No phone number, email address or postal address appears on the contact page or in the footer.
findings.user_impact: Customers who prefer to call, and customers who want proof the business exists before paying a deposit, have no way to do either.
findings.root_cause: The contact page offers only a form, which leaves buyers who want to call or verify the business with no route.
findings.intended_behavior: The form is meant to keep enquiries organised; it works for people who are comfortable submitting personal details to an unverified business.

evidence.description: The skeptical buyer looked for a phone number or address to verify the business and found only a form.
The low-literacy persona looked through the header, contact page and footer for a number to call and gave up.
TR-02 fails: the only contact route is a form.

steps: Look for any phone number, email address or postal address on the page.
Scroll to the footer and look again.
reproduction.expected: At least one direct contact route (phone or email) and a postal address are visible.
reproduction.actual: Only the contact form is present.

impact.reason: Two personas could not find a way to call, and the skeptic could not verify the business.

frequency.reason: Only visitors who want to call or verify are affected.

persistence.reason: The gap remains on every visit.

confidence.reason: Consistent across three sessions, but the evidence is text only and a contact link could exist in an image.

findings.baseline_comparison: Local businesses almost always show a phone number or email next to or beside the contact form.

remediation.strategy: Show a phone number, an email address and the shop address on the contact page and in the footer.

verification.notes: Re-fetched the contact page and footer: no phone, email or address in the page text.

findings.title: The inquiry form asks for phone and budget before showing any price
findings.description: The bespoke order form has nine fields, including a required phone number, an exact date and a budget range, and gives no price guidance anywhere on the route to it.
findings.user_impact: Visitors must commit personal details and guess a budget before they learn whether the bakery fits their needs, so some stop at the form.
findings.root_cause: The inquiry form demands nine fields including budget before any price is shown, which makes visitors commit before they can judge fit.
findings.intended_behavior: The form is meant to collect everything the bakers need to quote; it works for visitors who already trust the business and know their budget.

evidence.description: Nine fields are present; phone and budget range are required.
The budget options carry no explanation of what each range buys.
The first-time visitor hesitated at the budget field and said he had no idea what a cake costs.

steps: Read the form from top to bottom.
Try to decide what to enter in the budget field using only information on the site.
reproduction.expected: The visitor can choose a budget from information shown on the site.
reproduction.actual: No price information is available, so the budget field is a guess.

impact.reason: Visitors are asked to commit to a budget they cannot estimate.

frequency.reason: Every visitor who reaches the form meets the budget field.

persistence.reason: Visitors only fill the form once.

confidence.reason: Form structure is visible in the text; the actual drop-off cannot be measured.

findings.baseline_comparison: Custom-order forms from comparable bakeries usually ask four or five questions and show starting prices or examples nearby.

remediation.strategy: Cut the form to the fields needed for a first reply, make the budget optional with example price ranges, and show starting prices next to the form.

verification.notes: Re-fetched the order page: nine fields, phone and budget required, no price hint within two clicks.

findings.title: No price or price range appears anywhere on the site
findings.description: None of the product, collection or order pages state a price, a starting price or an example price.
findings.user_impact: Visitors cannot judge whether the bakery fits their budget, so some abandon and skeptical visitors read the silence as a warning sign.
findings.root_cause: The site publishes no price or starting price anywhere, which leaves visitors unable to judge whether the bakery fits their budget.
findings.intended_behavior: Pricing is probably withheld because every cake is custom; a 'from' price or example prices would still answer the question.

evidence.description: The first-time visitor searched seven pages for a price and gave up.
CT-01 fails for price: no page states a price, starting price or example.
The skeptical buyer noted that missing prices made them assume the cakes are expensive or the business is not serious.

steps: Open Collections, Bespoke Orders, FAQ and Journal.
Search each page for any amount of money.
reproduction.expected: At least a starting price or an example price per cake size.

impact.reason: A core purchase question cannot be answered on the site.

frequency.reason: Price is the first question for most buyers.

persistence.reason: The question stays open until the visitor contacts the bakery.

confidence.reason: Text search found no price; a price shown only in an image would be missed.

findings.baseline_comparison: Custom-cake bakeries commonly publish a starting price or a price table by size, even when each order is quoted individually.

remediation.strategy: Publish starting prices or a size-and-price table, and state that custom designs are quoted individually.

verification.notes: Searched the text of the collections, order, visit, FAQ and journal pages for currency symbols and amounts: none found.

findings.title: The same service has three different names
findings.description: The ordering service is called 'Bespoke Orders' in the page title, 'Custom Cakes' in the footer and 'Atelier requests' in the contact form's topic list.
findings.user_impact: Visitors cannot tell whether these are the same service, which adds doubt at the moment they are about to enquire.
findings.root_cause: The site uses three names for one service across the menu, footer and form, which makes visitors unsure they are in the right place.
findings.intended_behavior: Each label was probably written for its own context; together they read as three different offers.

evidence.location: Page title, footer, contact form topic list
evidence.description: Three different names appear for the same ordering route.
CL-10 fails: the contact form lists 'Atelier requests' as a separate topic from 'Custom Cakes'.

steps: Note the name of the ordering page in the page title.
Note the name in the footer.
Open the contact form and read the topic list.

impact.reason: It adds doubt but does not stop anyone.

frequency.reason: Anyone who reads the footer or the form sees it.

persistence.reason: A visitor works it out once.

confidence.reason: Two lens audits found it; no persona task depended on it.

findings.baseline_comparison: Consistent naming across navigation, headings and forms is standard on small business sites.

remediation.strategy: Choose one name (for example 'Custom cakes') and use it in the menu, page title, footer and form.

verification.notes: Confirmed the three names in the order page title, the footer link and the contact form topic list.

findings.title: The home page image carousel may auto-advance without a pause control
findings.description: The page structure describes a slideshow of seasonal cakes, but the text evidence does not show whether it moves on its own or whether a pause control exists.

evidence.description: The fetched content lists five slides inside one region and no visible pause or stop label.

findings.open_question: Does the home-page carousel advance automatically for more than five seconds without a visible pause control?
findings.resolution_path: Open the home page in a rendered browser for at least ten seconds and look for a pause control, or ask the developer.

findings.title: The footer has no sitemap link
findings.reason: Sitemap links are optional and the main navigation reaches every page within two clicks (L1-E02); no persona looked for one.

strengths.title: FAQ answers are short, plain and cover cancellation and allergens

evidence.description: Answers use everyday words, short paragraphs and name the notice period for changes.
The skeptical buyer found what happens on cancellation in one read and said it raised their trust.

strengths.why_it_works: It answers the questions buyers worry about in the words they use.
strengths.preserve_note: Keep the plain wording when adding prices; link the FAQ from the order form.

strengths.title: The order form says what happens next

evidence.description: A reply time and next step are stated next to the submit button.

strengths.why_it_works: Visitors know what to expect after sending personal details.
strengths.preserve_note: Keep this promise visible if the form is shortened.

strengths.title: Opening hours and address are plain text on the Visit page

evidence.description: Hours and address were found in two steps and are readable as text.

strengths.why_it_works: Two personas found hours and address on the first try.
strengths.preserve_note: Repeat the hours in the footer rather than moving them.
